target_stage: Delhi High Court appeal under s. 39 after remand to the Rent Control Tribunal for a finding on reasonably suitable residential accommodation

records.text: The appellant took on lease, the first floor of the premises in question from the respondent on January 22, 1964 on a monthly rent of Rs. 250.

The respondent who was the owner of the entire premises was then occupying the ground floor. The landlord filed an application, before the Rent Controller on November 26.1964 for eviction of the appellant from the portion in his occupation as lessee, on two grounds; (a) that the tenant has sub-let a part of the premises, and (b) that he required the premises bona fide for his occupation as a residence himself and his family members. The latter claim was based under cl.

The tenant opposed the claim of the landlord on both the grounds. He denied the allegation of sub-letting. He also contended that the landlord's requirement for his occupation was not bonafide. The tenant's plea was that the portion of the premises in his occupation was sufficient for his purpose. The Rent Controller accepted the plea of the tenant that there was no subletting. He also accepted his plea that the requirement of the landlord for his occupation was not bona fide.
It is the view of both the Tribunals that when eviction is asked for within about I I months of the letting, the claim of the landlord cannot be considered to be bonafide.

Before the High Court, counsel for both parties made a representation that the Rent Control Tribunal has not recorded a finding on the question whether the premises avaiable with the landlord can be considered to be "reasonably suitable residential accommodation" as contemplated by cl.

(e) of the proviso to cite13†s. 14 (1) . Hence they made a joint request to remand the case to the Tribunal for a finding on the said question on the basis of the evidence already on record. Accepting this joint request, the learned Judge remanded the case to the Tribunal.

The latter, after a consideration of the materials on record as well as the extent of the premises in the occupation of the landlord and also having due regard to the number of family members living with the latter, held, in his report dated May 4, 1970, that the portion of the premises in the occupation of the landlord was not reaso- nably sufficient for a family consisting of the landlord, his wife, his son, son's wife and their children.
On this basis, he recorded a finding that the premises in the occupation of the respondent were not reasonably suitable for his residence.

target_stage: Landlord's appeal under Section 38 of the Delhi Rent Control Act from the CCJ-cum-ARC judgment dated 15.03.2019.
target_court: Principal District & Sessions Judge (Central), Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi

records.text: 2. It was the case of the eviction petitioner - landlord that she had rented out the premises bearing Shop No. 15, in property no. 4415, Gali Bahuji, Pahari Dheeraj, Delhi-110006 to one Sh. Ramesh Kumar on 06.01.1987. However, the said tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar had parted with possession and sub-let and assigned the same initially to one Sh. Ghanshyam Dass and subsequently to Sh. Bhagwan Dass, who were his father and brother respectively.

The current sub-lessee Bhagwant Dass was pleaded to be opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. It was also pleaded that the aforesaid Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a tenant in his independent rights of the petitioner in shop no. 6 in the same property and was using the shop no. 6 as godown and had shifted the counter from shop no. 6 to shop no. 15. Necessary permission for institution of eviction petition from the competent Slum Authority had been taken.

2.1 Petition was resisted by present respondent - tenant Sh. Ramesh Kumar and it was denied that the property had been sub let by him to his brother Bhagwan Dass. It was pleaded by the respondent that he is occupying the demised shop as a tenant and additionally conducting his business from shop no. 5765, Sikli Gran, Factory Road, Nabi Karim, New Delhi-110055.

As regards the respondent's brother Bhagwan Dass, it was further case of the respondent that his brother Bhagwan Dass was helping him in opening and closing the shop and dealing with the customers. However, it was denied that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was a sub tenant in the suit premises. Petitioner was pleaded to be receiving rent from the respondent.

3. Petitioner in support of her case examined her attorney, Sh. M.L. Jain as PW-1, who supported the petition. Petitioner also examined two other witnesses, who were shopkeepers having their shops in the vicinity. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was running the shop and not respondent Sh. Ramesh Kumar.

4. Respondent in support of his case examined himself as RW-1 and his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass, the alleged sub-lessee, as RW-2. Both the witnesses deposed that Sh. Bhagwan Dass was working as an employee and drawing a salary of Rs. 10,000/- per month. The fact of Sh. Bhagwan Dass operating the shop and being in possession of key thereof was admitted. No proof of any other employee was produced. Salary vouchers of payment of salary to Sh. Bhagwan Dass were also not proved.

5. Trial Court by the impugned judgment took the view that the fact of sub tenancy was not established. Trial court held that it was only a privilege or a licence by the tenant in favour of his brother to use the premises, which licence or privilege could be terminated at the sweet will and pleasure of respondent. Therefore, the arrangement did not amount to assignment or parting with the possession.
Further, it was the trial court's view that Bhagwan Dass was not a stranger or outsider but a family member of the respondent, therefore, sub-letting cannot be inferred.
